r: KOR 1010 builds elementary Korean across listening, speaking, reading, and writing, with heavy weight on oral communication in varied socio-cultural contexts. The instrumental question is whether AI substitutes for a student personally acquiring these four skills. Task-exposure research classifies translators and interpreters among the most-exposed occupations, which pushes down the case for learning Korean purely to perform translation tasks. But this course's applied work is embodied, real-time oral production and listening comprehension — pronunciation, conversational exchange, live interpersonal understanding — categories task-exposure frameworks do not treat as directly automatable, and F3 embodiment stays moderate rather than low. The course carries a GT-Pathways oral-communication designation, an institutional transfer mandate independent of AI capability, and functions as prerequisite scaffolding for the beginning-Korean sequence. At 24 months, with limited real-world diffusion of AI into classroom language pedagogy and the embodied oral-skill core intact, the instrumental need to take this course is not eroded. Rating: Low.

By 2031, real-time AI translation and conversational agents will be highly capable and widely diffused, seriously eroding the instrumental rationale for learning Korean specifically to perform translation, basic lookup, or scripted cross-language exchange — a genuine downward pressure given how strongly task-exposure research rates translation and interpretation work. What survives is the value of a student directly producing and comprehending spoken and written Korean in real time, embodied interpersonal contexts where the learner's own competence matters rather than a mediating tool, plus the course's continuing GT-Pathways oral-communication mandate and its role as scaffolding for the beginning-sequence. That transfer requirement and foundational function cap the erosion rather than eliminate it. Observed-usage data confirms AI is now heavily used for language and writing tasks generally, reinforcing the substitution pressure on translation-adjacent work. The rating rises to Medium: the translation-as-task rationale is substantially automatable, but embodied communicative competence and the institutional lock hold the course at a middle band rather than High.

A decade out, seamless AI-mediated translation and interpretation are pervasive across text and speech, and the instrumental case for studying Korean as a translation tool is substantially eroded — one of the more clear-cut examples of AI performing the applied task the course historically supported. Capability-trend evidence points toward continued rapid improvement in multilingual, real-time systems over this horizon. What remains instrumentally defensible is direct human-to-human communication in Korean for interpersonal, cultural, and real-time embodied contexts machine mediation does not fully substitute, together with the GT-Pathways general-education requirement, which in the central case still governs the transfer curriculum. The rating holds Medium rather than falling to High, capped by that institutional designation and the residual embodied-communication value, rather than rising toward Low. Confidence is lower than for non-language courses: reasonable analysts could argue the erosion runs deeper by 2036 if ambient real-time translation becomes normalized enough to blunt even face-to-face motivation for language acquisition, and the ten-year forecast carries uncertainty.
KOR 1010.d: Elementary Korean I is designed for students who have no prior knowledge in Korean. It emphasizes the development of four basic skills (listening, speaking, reading, and writing) in various socio-cultural contexts. The course can serve as the first half of a two-semester sequence in Beginning Korean and is designed to match the curriculum requirements of existing Asian Languages and Cultures programs.
